title: Making History Relevant
author: Brown, Lauren
source: The US History Teachers Lounge, July 31, 2026
summary: Lauren Brown argues against the ubiquitous teacher impulse to 'make history relevant' by connecting everything to students' existing lives, contending that this strategy both trivialises history and misunderstands what students actually need from an education. Drawing on a 2016 MiddleWeb essay, she shows how the relevance framework carries a utilitarian bias that reduces the worth of knowledge to its immediate applicability in students' current lives. Brown argues that students are naturally curious about the world beyond their experience, and that the goal of history education is to introduce them to things they don't yet know — not to domesticate the past into a mirror of the present. She uses Holocaust education as a case study: asking students to connect the deportation of Jewish families to a time they moved house is not empathetic but epistemically reckless. The article advocates instead for helping students understand why history is interesting, puzzling, and consequential on its own terms.
points: One reason I hate the phrase 'making history relevant' is the utilitarian bias of it — it suggests that something must be useful to make it worthy of our attention.

Making history relevant should not mean shrinking the past until it resembles students' existing experience — it means helping students see why the past is interesting and consequential in its own right.
Students want to know things about the world because human beings are naturally curious — the goal is to introduce them to what they don't yet know, not to validate what they already know.
Asking students to think about a time they moved when studying the deportation of Jewish families risks minimising the historical reality and suggesting the analogy is appropriate when it is not.
The goal of educating students is to introduce them to the wider world of which they are a part — not merely to connect everything back to their current lives, which might still be rather closed.

In their book, The Disengaged Teen: Helping Kids Learn Better, Feel Better, co-authors Jenny Anderson and Rebecca Winthrop mention some studies by psychology professor Johnmarshall Reeve that found kids were more motivated and learned more when students felt like they had agency over their learning.

I had a student whose great uncle was Senator Glass of the Glass-Steagall Act, countless students whose families were part of the Great Migration, including one whose grandfather was Emmett Till’s first cousin and was in Money, Mississippi the night Till was kidnapped and murdered!

It is to use history to make their worlds larger—to help them recognize that the places they live, the questions they argue about, and the society they have inherited are all part of a much longer, more complicated and endlessly fascinating human story.

It shows that you have learned more over time and now you recognize the mistake of asking your students to write an essay on “whether or not Truman should have used the atomic bomb” because it encourages ahistorical thinking.
